```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)
# non-ASCII characters in output and plots under a "C" locale
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
```

The [classical definition](../probability-definition/index.qmd) $P(A) = N(A)/N(\Omega)$ only works when the sample space is finite and the outcomes are equally likely. But what about a loaded die, the number of customers at a checkout, which can be arbitrarily large, or the arrival time of the first customer, which takes uncountably many values? In 1933 Andrey Kolmogorov gave an answer that still stands: instead of saying *how* to compute a probability, we state **which rules it must obey**.

## Probability spaces

A **probability space** is a triple $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$, where:

1. $\Omega$ is the sample space of the experiment.
2. $\mathcal{F}$ is the collection of events to which we assign probabilities.
3. $P$ is a function that assigns a number $P(A)$ to every event $A \in \mathcal{F}$.

### Why we need the collection $\mathcal{F}$

When $\Omega$ is finite or countable, we take $\mathcal{F}$ to be **all** subsets of $\Omega$, and there is no problem. But when $\Omega$ is uncountable, for example the interval $[0, 1]$, it can be proved that some subsets are so "pathological" that no consistent probability can be assigned to them (the Vitali set is the classic example). So we restrict ourselves to a collection $\mathcal{F}$ that is a **sigma-algebra**, meaning that:

- it contains $\Omega$,
- whenever it contains $A$, it also contains the complement $A'$,
- whenever it contains $A_1, A_2, \ldots$, it also contains their union $\bigcup_{n} A_n$.

In plain terms, $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under the operations we perform on events: anything built from events using complements, unions and intersections is itself an event. In practical problems we rarely need to think about the sigma-algebra; all intervals and their unions belong to it.

## The three axioms

The function $P$ is called a **probability** if it satisfies **Kolmogorov's axioms**:

**(K1) Non-negativity.** $P(A) \ge 0$ for every $A \in \mathcal{F}$.

**(K2) Normalisation.** $P(\Omega) = 1$.

**(K3) Countable additivity.** If $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ are pairwise disjoint ($A_i \cap A_j = \varnothing$ for $i \ne j$), then

$$P\Big(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\Big) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(A_n).$$

That is all. Nothing about equally likely outcomes, relative frequencies or how a number is computed. Any function satisfying these three rules is a legitimate probability.

## Every rule from three axioms

The rules from the previous post, which there came from counting, can now be proved for every probability:

- **$P(\varnothing) = 0$.** Take $A_1 = \Omega$ and $A_2 = A_3 = \cdots = \varnothing$, which are pairwise disjoint. By (K3), $P(\Omega) = P(\Omega) + \sum_{n \ge 2} P(\varnothing)$, so $P(\varnothing) = 0$.
- **Finite additivity.** If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, take $A_1 = A$, $A_2 = B$ and all the rest empty: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
- **Complement.** $A$ and $A'$ are disjoint with union $\Omega$, so $P(A) + P(A') = 1$. Since $P(A') \ge 0$, it also follows that $P(A) \le 1$.
- **Monotonicity.** If $A \subseteq B$, then $B = A \cup (B - A)$ with disjoint pieces, so $P(B) = P(A) + P(B - A) \ge P(A)$.
- **Union.** Write $A \cup B = A \cup (B - A)$ and $B = (A \cap B) \cup (B - A)$, always with disjoint pieces. Subtracting the two equations gives
  $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B).$$

All of probability theory, from distributions to the central limit theorem, is built on these three axioms.

## Examples of probability spaces

**The classical definition as a special case.** If $\Omega$ is finite and we set $P(A) = N(A)/N(\Omega)$, the three axioms hold. The classical definition is therefore **one** example of a probability, not its definition.

**A loaded die.** Give each face $i$ a weight $p_i \ge 0$ with $p_1 + \cdots + p_6 = 1$, and define $P(A) = \sum_{i \in A} p_i$. The axioms hold even though the outcomes are not equally likely. In the explorer below you build your own die: you give relative weights to the faces, the page normalises them so that (K2) holds, and it computes the probability of any event you choose.

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Build your own die
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
presets14 = ({
  "Fair die": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
  "Die with P(1) = P(3) = P(5) = 2P(2) = 4P(4) = 2P(6)": [4, 2, 4, 1, 4, 2],
  "Die that favours 6": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 5],
  "Die that never shows 1": [0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
})
viewof preset14 = Inputs.select(Object.keys(presets14), {label: "Start from", value: "Die with P(1) = P(3) = P(5) = 2P(2) = 4P(4) = 2P(6)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof w14 = Inputs.form(presets14[preset14].map((v, i) =>
  Inputs.range([0, 10], {label: `Weight of face ${i + 1}`, step: 1, value: v})))
viewof ev14 = Inputs.checkbox([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], {label: "Event A", value: [2, 4, 6], format: x => `${x}`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const gcd = (a, b) => b === 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b);
  const frac = (a, b) => { if (b === 0) return "—"; if (a === 0) return "0"; if (a === b) return "1"; const g = gcd(a, b); return `${a / g}/${b / g}`; };
  const fmt = x => x.toLocaleString("en-GB", {minimumFractionDigits: 3, maximumFractionDigits: 3});
  const total = w14.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0);
  if (total === 0) return html`<div class="ix-warn">All weights are 0: there is no way to make P(Ω) = 1. Give at least one face a positive weight.</div>`;
  const data = w14.map((w, i) => ({face: i + 1, p: w / total, inA: ev14.includes(i + 1), w}));
  const wA = data.filter(d => d.inA).reduce((s, d) => s + d.w, 0);
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    height: 220, marginLeft: 45,
    x: {label: "Face", type: "band"}, y: {label: "↑ Probability", grid: true, domain: [0, Math.max(0.5, ...data.map(d => d.p))]},
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(data, {x: "face", y: "p", fill: d => d.inA ? "#4e79a7" : "#c9d1da"}),
      Plot.text(data, {x: "face", y: "p", text: d => frac(d.w, total), dy: -8}),
      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]
  });
  return html`<div>${chart}
    <table class="ix-tbl">
      <tr><td>Sum of probabilities (K2)</td><td><b>1</b> ✓ (weights divided by ${total})</td></tr>
      <tr><td>P(A), A = {${ev14.join(", ")}}</td><td><b>${frac(wA, total)} ≈ ${fmt(wA / total)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>P(A′) = 1 − P(A)</td><td><b>${frac(total - wA, total)} ≈ ${fmt(1 - wA / total)}</b></td></tr>
    </table>
    <div class="ix-note">Blue bars belong to event A. Each probability is the face's weight divided by the sum of the weights.</div></div>`;
}
```
:::

With the default die, the probability of an even number is $5/17$, as we computed in the previous post. Try the die that never shows 1 as well: there $P(\{1\}) = 0$, which is perfectly legitimate.

**A countable sample space.** For the number $X$ of customers arriving at a checkout in one minute, a simple model is $P(X = k) = (1 - q)\,q^k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, with $0 < q < 1$. (K2) holds thanks to the geometric series $\sum_{k \ge 0} (1 - q) q^k = 1$, and (K3) lets us add up infinitely many terms:

```{r}
#| label: geometric
q <- 0.7
k <- 0:500
p <- (1 - q) * q^k
sum(p)                 # ≈ 1: (K2) holds
sum(p[k >= 4])         # P(X ≥ 4) as a sum of infinitely many disjoint events
q^4                    # the same number from the formula
```

**An uncountable sample space.** Pick a point of $[0, 1]$ "uniformly": the probability that it lands in an interval $[a, b]$ is its length, $b - a$. Then every **single** point has probability $0$, since a point is an interval of length $0$. Yet some point will be chosen! So **$P(A) = 0$ does not mean that $A$ is impossible**. The converse always holds, $P(\varnothing) = 0$, but not this. We will meet this again with continuous random variables.

## Why there is no "random natural number"

A well-known question asks: "Pick a natural number at random. What is the probability that it is divisible by 3?" The intuitive answer is $1/3$. Axiom (K3), however, shows that the question, as stated, makes no sense.

If "at random" means that all natural numbers are equally likely, then $P(\{n\}) = c$ for every $n$. The sets $\{1\}, \{2\}, \ldots$ are disjoint with union $\mathbb{N}$, so by (K2) and (K3):

$$1 = P(\mathbb{N}) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c = \begin{cases} 0, & c = 0, \\ \infty, & c > 0. \end{cases}$$

Both cases are impossible. **There is no uniform probability on the natural numbers.**

So what is the $1/3$? It is the **asymptotic density** of the multiples of 3: their proportion among $1, 2, \ldots, N$ as $N$ grows.

```{r}
#| label: density
N <- 10^(1:6)
data.frame(N = N, `proportion of multiples of 3` = sapply(N, function(n) mean((1:n) %% 3 == 0)),
           check.names = FALSE)
```

The proportion tends to $1/3$, but density is not probability: it is not countably additive, since every single number has density $0$ while $\mathbb{N}$ has density $1$. To speak correctly about probability here, we must define the experiment, for example "pick a number uniformly from $1$ to $N$", in which case the answer is $\lfloor N/3 \rfloor / N$.

## Key takeaways

- A **probability space** $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ consists of the sample space, the events (a sigma-algebra) and the probability function.
- The **three axioms** are non-negativity, $P(\Omega) = 1$ and countable additivity. Every probability rule is proved from them.
- The classical definition is a special case. Non-uniform, countable and continuous models all fit in the same framework.
- **$P(A) = 0$ does not mean impossible**, and **there is no uniform probability on $\mathbb{N}$**.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.**

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz14 = [
  {q: "Which of the following is NOT one of Kolmogorov's axioms, but is proved from them?",
   opts: ["P(Ω) = 1", "P(A) ≥ 0", "P(A′) = 1 − P(A)", "Countable additivity"], ans: 2,
   why: "The complement rule follows from (K2) and (K3), because A and A′ are disjoint with union Ω."},
  {q: "A and B are disjoint. Can we have P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5?",
   opts: ["Yes", "No"], ans: 1,
   why: "That would give P(A ∪ B) = 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1 > 1, which is impossible."},
  {q: "If P(A) = 0, must A be the empty set?",
   opts: ["Yes, always", "Not necessarily"], ans: 1,
   why: "When a point of [0, 1] is chosen uniformly, every single point has probability 0 without being impossible."},
  {q: "Can we give every natural number the same probability?",
   opts: ["Yes, 1/∞", "No, it contradicts the axioms"], ans: 1,
   why: "A constant c > 0 sums to ∞, while c = 0 sums to 0. Neither gives P(ℕ) = 1."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz14.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz14.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```
:::

**2.** Prove **Boole's inequality** from the axioms: $P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B)$.

**3.** Prove that $P(A - B) = P(A) - P(A \cap B)$.

**4.** In the model $P(X = k) = (1 - q)\,q^k$ with $q = 0.7$, what is the probability of at most 2 customers?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. By the union rule, $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \le P(A) + P(B)$, since $P(A \cap B) \ge 0$ by (K1).
3. $A - B$ and $A \cap B$ are disjoint with union $A$, so $P(A) = P(A - B) + P(A \cap B)$.
4. $P(X \le 2) = 0.3 \cdot (1 + 0.7 + 0.49) = 0.657$, or equivalently $1 - q^3 = 1 - 0.343$.
:::
